title: Quotient Groups
short: When N is normal, the cosets of N form a group G/N with (aN)(bN) = abN, of order |G|/|N|.
trouble: Students take the order of a coset to be the order of its representative: in ℤ₁₂/⟨4⟩ the coset 1 + ⟨4⟩ has order 4, while 1 has order 12 in ℤ₁₂.

blocks.html: Arithmetic mod $n$ is arithmetic with cosets of $n\mathbb{Z}$: we add classes by adding any representatives. The same works in any group, provided the subgroup is normal.

Theorem. If $N$ is normal in $G$, the rule $(aN)(bN) = abN$ is well defined, and with it the set $G/N$ of cosets is a group, the quotient group (or factor group). Its identity is $eN = N$, the inverse of $aN$ is $a^{-1}N$, and $|G/N| = |G|/|N|$.
Proof of well-definedness. Suppose $aN = a'N$ and $bN = b'N$, so $a' = an_{1}$ and $b' = bn_{2}$ with $n_{1}, n_{2} \in N$. Then $$a'b' = a\,n_{1}\,b\,n_{2} = ab\,(b^{-1}n_{1}b)\,n_{2}.$$ Since $N$ is normal, $b^{-1}n_{1}b \in N$, so $a'b' \in abN$ and $a'b'N = abN$. The group axioms are inherited from $G$: $(aN)(bN)(cN) = abcN$ either way, $(eN)(aN) = aN$, and $(a^{-1}N)(aN) = N$. $\square$

Normality is exactly what makes this work. In $S_{3}$ with $H = \{e, (1\;2)\}$, the cosets $(1\;3)H$ and $(1\;3)(1\;2)H$ are equal, yet multiplying each by $(1\;3)H$ "by representatives" gives two different cosets. With a non-normal subgroup there is no quotient group.

blocks.name: aa-cayley
blocks.cap: The Cayley table of $D_{4}$ with rows and columns grouped by the cosets of the normal subgroup $\{e, r^{2}\}$, each cell colored by the coset of its entry. Every $2 \times 2$ block is one color, so the blocks multiply like the four cosets: the table of $D_{4}/\{e, r^{2}\}$.

blocks.title: Computing in $\mathbb{Z}_{12}/\langle 4 \rangle$
blocks.q: In $G/N = \mathbb{Z}_{12}/\langle 4 \rangle$, compute $(3 + N) + (2 + N)$ and find the order of $1 + N$.
steps: $1 + N$, $2 + N$, $3 + N$, $4 + N = N$: the order of $1 + N$ is $4$, although $|1| = 12$ in $\mathbb{Z}_{12}$.

blocks.title: A quotient of $D_{4}$
steps: Each non-identity coset squares to $N$: $r^{2} \in N$, $s^{2} = e$, $(rs)^{2} = e$.
A group of order 4 in which every element has order at most 2 is not cyclic.
blocks.a: A non-cyclic group of order $4$, like $U(8)$.

blocks.html: Taking the order of a coset to be the order of its representative. The order of $aN$ is the least $m$ with $a^{m} \in N$, which can be much smaller than $|a|$: in $\mathbb{Z}_{12}/\langle 4 \rangle$ the coset $1 + N$ has order $4$, while $1$ has order $12$ in $\mathbb{Z}_{12}$. By Lagrange, the order of $aN$ divides $|G/N|$.
For a normal subgroup $N$, cosets multiply by representatives, $(aN)(bN) = abN$, giving the quotient group $G/N$ of order $|G|/|N|$. The order of $aN$ is the least $m$ with $a^{m} \in N$.
